 Jensen Huang's future in the balance after reports of another affair. Here's the latest
 By Deva Lee 
 Nvidia’s board is meeting to discuss the future of founder and CEO Jensen Huang , two sources told CNN, after reports that he had an affair with Kimberly Powell , vice president of healthcare at the chip behemoth.
 There was some expectation among Trump administration insiders that Huang would be ousted, the sources said.
 Mounting scandal: Earlier this week, Nvidia’s board said it would investigate whether Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort” amid reports that he had a separate relationship with Alice Huang, a woman US officials believe to be a Chinese spy. The CEO apologized Sunday for an extramarital affair, although he did not name the other party. Here’s what we know about Alice Huang. 
 Nvidia’s Code of Conduct lays out how employees, business partners and managers are expected to act with integrity and avoid conflicts of interest.
 Stocks tumble: Nvidia shares dropped sharply in after-hours trading. The tech giant has shed more than $300 billion in market value this week alone.
 Trump’s take: President Donald Trump has stood by Huang, saying Monday that he spoke with the CEO, who denied knowing the woman was allegedly a spy. In May, Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefed Trump on intelligence that Huang was in a relationship with a potential Chinese spy as they traveled to China, a source told CNN. Trump on Monday publicly denied knowing about the allegations at that time.
 The scandal comes as Trump prepares for a trip to Shenzhen, the Chinese tech and innovation hub, where he is expected to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping. The allegations that China’s spy service targeted Huang will have far-reaching implications for the US-China race to dominate AI. Here’s why. 
 Who could lead Nvidia next? Analysts are now questioning who could replace the CEO, since the company has no clear public succession plan in place .
 Here’s a timeline of the scandal , and the major company milestones that preceded it.
 CNN’s Hadas Gold, John Towfighi, Stephanie Yang, Anna Cooban, Clare Duffy, Jessie Yeung, Isaac Yee, Kylie Atwood and Kevin Liptak contributed reporting.

 Who's on the board of directors discussing Huang's fate?
 By Jessie Yeung 
 All eyes are on Nvidia’s board of directors, which is meeting late Wednesday night to discuss the fate of scandal-hit CEO Jensen Huang – with the company’s shares dropping sharply, and no clear successor.
 The board is made up of 11 directors, including Huang himself. In an unusual arrangement, there is no board chair, according to the lineup on Nvidia’s website.
 The directors include heavy hitters from various sectors – former executives from global brands like Taco Bell, Pepsi-Cola and the NFL – as well as academics, scientists and financial leaders.
 Four of them have been with the company, and known Huang, since the 1990s. The others joined between 2013 to 2026.
 The fact that many directors share a long history with Huang has raised questions about whether they can make objective decisions about his future at the company and the ongoing investigation, Reuters reported. 
 On Tuesday, Nvidia’s board announced it had retained high-profile New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to lead the investigation into whether Huang was a target of a foreign intelligence effort.

 Jensen Huang has long been a bridge between US and China
 By Jessie Yeung 
 Jensen Huang waves as he prepares to depart the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, China on May 14. 
 Alex Wong/Getty Images 
 Nvidia chief Jensen Huang may have unwittingly found himself in the middle of a spy scandal involving Chinese spies and American chips – but he has long positioned himself as a bridge between the two rival countries and top economies.
 Huang moved from Taiwan to Thailand as a child and then to the United States – a background that gave him the language and cultural skills needed to navigate business both in the US and in China.
 As Huang grew closer to President Donald Trump, he also gained visibility with Beijing; when Chinese leader Xi Jinping made a state visit in September, Huang was among several top tech executives having dinner at the head table with Trump and Xi.
 And Huang joined Trump during a layover in Alaska on the way to Beijing in May, accompanying him and his top aides on Air Force One. A source told CNN that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had briefed Trump on intelligence that Huang was in a relationship with a potential Chinese spy before the Nvidia CEO got on the plane – though Trump on Monday publicly denied knowing about the allegations at that time.
 It was during that visit to Beijing that Huang charmed much of the Chinese internet – and watchers around the world – when he took himself on an impromptu food tour of the Chinese capital.
 “Jensen, how do you like China?” a woman is heard asking him in one video. The Nvidia CEO responded: “I love China.”
 Trump is set to visit China again next week. When asked on Sunday whether he would bring Huang along on his trip, the president responded, “I don’t know, but I’d certainly take him.” It’s not clear if Huang plans to go.

 Democrats urge Trump officials to preserve Nvidia documents, raise questions of inaction
 By Jessie Yeung 
 Elizabeth Warren attends the Senate Banking Committee on Capitol Hill in Washington, DC on July 15. 
 Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images 
 Two Democratic senators, Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons, issued a letter to several top Trump administration officials on Wednesday, asking them to preserve all Nvidia-related documents – and questioning whether they had known about the allegations surrounding Jensen Huang and failed to act.
 The letter was addressed to Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, urging their three respective departments to preserve all documents “regarding the export of NVIDIA’s advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China.”
 Huang is under intense scrutiny after reports that he had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, of no relation, who was working as a spy for China.
 “Reports suggest that officials within the government – including at the White House, State Department, and Commerce Department – were aware of concerns about NVIDIA, its relationship with (Alice Huang’s company) Megaspeed, and the suspected Chinese intelligence operation, yet did not move to block the continued flow of advanced AI chips to Megaspeed or other companies affiliated with the suspected operative,” said Warren and Coons in the letter.
 They also asked the officials to brief Congress on what risks the alleged foreign intelligence operation could have posed to the US’ national security.

 For Taiwan, a mutually beneficial relationship just got complicated
 Analysis by Will Ripley and Wayne Chang in Taipei
 Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang signs a magazine cover for his fans in Taipei, Taiwan on January 17, 2025. 
 Ann Wang/Reuters 
 Jensen Huang has spent years cultivating a personal relationship with Taiwan, the island of his birth.
 Whenever he visits, he eats at local restaurants, speaks comfortably in Taiwanese Hokkien as well as Mandarin, poses for endless selfies and signs autographs – including at least once across a female fan’s chest – turning routine business trips into media events.
 For many here, Nvidia’s success feels partly their own – reflected in the surging stock prices in Taiwan and the booming export figures driven by huge demand for AI.
 And Huang – who was born in the city of Tainan and spent the first five years of his life on the island – is one of their own. He has lavishly praised Taiwan and given it massive global visibility.
 Tim Culpan, a technology journalist who has known Huang for more than 25 years, says the affair itself isn’t necessarily what troubles Taiwanese people most; it’s the reported connection to Chinese intelligence.
 “It was with the enemy. That’s the part that hurts Taiwanese,” Culpan told CNN.
 Up until now it’s been a mutually beneficial relationship. Taiwan produces the advanced chips underpinning Nvidia’s dominance, while facing daily pressure from Beijing, which considers Taiwan part of its territory. The possibility that someone close to Huang was working for Chinese intelligence touches a particularly raw nerve.
 There’s money at stake, too. Many Taiwanese own shares in Nvidia or its local suppliers. TSMC – the island’s crown jewel, which produces more than 90% of the world’s advanced microchips – makes up roughly 40% of Taiwan’s benchmark stock index alone.
 Nvidia is also investing more than $1 billion in a new Taipei headquarters, expected to open in 2030 – a major bet on Taiwan that city officials insist remains on track despite the scandal.
 Huang’s popularity won’t disappear overnight. But in Taiwan, where business, technology and homeland security are inseparable, this is no longer just a story about his private life.

 Why Nvidia’s chips are so sought after by China
 By Jessie Yeung and Isaac Yee 
 Ian Buck, vice president of accelerated computing at Nvidia Corp., during the Nvidia GTC conference in San Jose, California, US, on March 18. 
 David Paul/Bloomberg/Getty Images 
 The allegations that China’s spy service targeted Jensen Huang through a woman he had an affair with will have far-reaching implications for the US-China race to dominate AI.
 At the center of this fight are Nvidia’s AI chips, which China has long sought to access.
 For years, the US government has restricted China’s access to advanced American technology in an effort to slow its progress on AI. During his first term, Trump imposed restrictions on Chinese giant Huawei; the Biden administration introduced further export controls on US-made semiconductors, advanced chips and chip-making equipment.
 Since then, China’s chip technology has made significant strides. Experts say Huawei has developed chips with performance comparable to — and in some cases surpassing — some of Nvidia’s chips.
 Perhaps sensing that China is getting ahead anyway, regardless of export controls, the Trump administration reversed its stance last year and approved the sale of a key Nvidia chip, the H20. At the time, Trump argued the H20 was “obsolete” as it lags behind Nvidia’s more advanced Blackwell or H100 chips – which are still blocked.
 Despite China’s progress, Nvidia’s chips remain highly coveted by Chinese companies, and are sometimes smuggled in. Alice Huang is alleged to have helped facilitate this smuggling.
 Just last month, a Chinese university linked with the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) bought two of Nvidia’s powerful H200 chips from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology, circumventing a US-imposed blocklist on the institution, according to a filing on the university’s website.
 Reuters first reported the purchase. Neither the Northwestern Polytechnical University nor Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology responded to phone calls from CNN seeking comment.

 By Matt Stiles and Alex Leeds Matthews 
 Nvidia’s board is reportedly meeting Wednesday evening to discuss CEO Jensen Huang’s future as its leader, following a rough few days for the embattled CEO. Here is how Huang, and Nvidia, got here.

 Wall Street weighs in on Nvidia
 By John Towfighi 
 A television broadcasts Nvidia Corp news on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York, US, on Monday. 
 Michael Nagle/Bloomberg/Getty Images 
 Nvidia shares ( NVDA ) were down 8.6% in after-hours trading as of 8 p.m. ET as Wall Street digests the developments surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
 “If Jensen Huang is ousted as is expected, an already challenging environment for Nvidia investors and employees will become considerably more difficult,” Mike O’Rourke, chief market strategist at JonesTrading, told CNN in an email.
 “Nvidia is currently the most important company in the world,” he said. “The new CEO will need to make an extensive appraisal of the company and Jensen’s successor will not have the same latitude or deference to pursue circular deals and pursue aggressive sales tactics.”
 Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., wrote in a note that he thinks “the writing is on the wall and Jensen’s days at Nvidia could be numbered.”
 “While Jensen is the hearts and lungs of the Nvidia story… the company and its leading edge GPU technology will go on and it does not change the entrenched position Nvidia has in the AI Revolution chip arms race,” Ives said.
 While Nvidia shares tumbled, shares of other chipmakers rose: Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD ) gained 4.3% and Broadcom ( AVGO ) gained 2.4%.
 Huang is at “the epicenter for deal making in the AI complex,” said Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of the Founders 100 ETF, a fund focused on founder-led companies. “Without him, that goes away, and so it opens up more opportunities for AMD, more opportunities for [Broadcom].”
 “If Jensen the kingmaker is gone, it could really become a more free-for-all playing field,” Monaghan told CNN. “We still need to see what the board’s going to do.”

 Nvidia scandal comes before Trump's high-stakes trip to Shenzhen
 By Jessie Yeung 
 Visitors take photos at an APEC themed flower display in front of the Qianhai Exhibition Hall in Shenzhen, China, on Tuesday. 
 China News Service/China News Service/China News Service via Getty Ima 
 Jensen Huang’s spy scandal and the spectacular fallout for Nvidia comes at a fraught time for US-China relations, and a sensitive one for the White House, as President Donald Trump prepares for a trip to Shenzhen.
 The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit will take place next week in the southern Chinese tech and innovation hub, where Trump is expected to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the third time so far this year. 
 Bilateral relations remain fraught. A fragile trade truce between the world’s two biggest economies will expire in January, and analysts say the risk of additional tariffs and other trade barriers will continue to loom in the new year.
 Other experts say that Trump might be more willing to play hard ball during future negotiations, now that the midterm elections are over, and Trump no longer has to worry about how Chinese countermeasure might sway voters.
 At the Shenzhen summit, Xi and Trump may also hold a historic meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines. Last month, Trump said he was open to this idea, telling reporters: “We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization … I’m sure we’d talk about other things like trade too.”

 "Jensen has created a black eye moment." Wall Street tech analyst says CEO likely must go
 By Matt Egan 
 Dan Ives speaks at a conference in New York on October 8. 
 Evan Agostini/Invision/AP 
 Dan Ives, one of the biggest AI bulls on Wall Street, says the “writing is on the wall” that Jensen Huang’s days leading Nvidia are likely numbered.
 “Jensen has created a black eye moment for himself and Nvidia and now has created a spider web of complexity that Wall Street, Silicon Valley, DC and the global tech ecosystem are trying to figure out what is next,” Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, wrote in a report to clients Wednesday night.
 Ives cited The New York Times report that Huang had an affair with a direct report.
 “The reality is that the old Jensen is now gone in the eyes of the public, customer and technology world,” the tech analyst wrote. “Nvidia likely now has to move on without Jensen at the helm, which seemed like a Twilight Zone episode narrative before Sunday afternoon when the news broke.”
 Huang is widely viewed as irreplaceable and Nvidia failed to groom a successor who could step in, a decision that now looks highly questionable.
 If the board pushes out Huang, it risks spooking already-rattled investors about who will steer the ship. With Huang in charge, Nvidia is worth $300 per share, compared with $225 without him, Ives says.
 While Ives said Huang is “not replaceable by another CEO or group of interim executives,” he expressed confidence in Nvidia and its leading edge GPU technology. “The company will navigate this turmoil and get through to the other side and remain a core foundational piece of the AI revolution,” Ives said.

 "We’re past the tipping point." Ex-SEC chair says Nvidia is now likely to oust Jensen Huang
 By Matt Egan 
 A screengrab from a video obtained on November 9, 2026 shows a woman identified as Alice Huang attending a dinner with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at a restaurant in Taipei, Taiwan on May 22, 2025. 
 CTI/Handout/Reuters 
 The allegation that Nvidia’s Jensen Huang had a second affair is likely to force the board of directors to oust the rockstar CEO, former Securities and Exchange Commission chairman Gary Gensler told CNN on Wednesday evening.
 “This feels like we’re past the tipping point,” Gensler said. “It has become far more untenable to keep him. It’s now at that breaking point.”
 Gensler, now a professor at MIT, said Nvidia was already dealing with a massive public relation crisis caused by Huang’s admitted affair.
 US officials have told CNN that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, who they have concluded is a Chinese spy.
 “At some point in time, it’s too much weight to hold up,” Gensler said. “If he misled the board in any step of the way, the board says, ‘We’ve got to look out for our shareholders, our own reputation.’”
 Alice Huang was an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer under investigation for allegedly diverting cutting-edge chips to China.
 Gensler said Megaspeed appears to be a front company, masking its true backers. “It’s a cardboard cut-out of a company,” he said. “It’s like a stage front on a Hollywood lot.”

 Nvidia has shed more than $300 billion in market value this week
 By John Towfighi 
 Nvidia Corp news on a chyron at the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York, US, on Monday. 
 Michael Nagle/Bloomberg/Getty Images 
 The controversy surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has knocked the company’s stock, wiping off hundreds of billions of dollars in market value.
 Nvidia shares were down 6.92% on the week as of Wednesday’s market close, erasing $311 billion in market value.
 With Nvidia’s 8% after-hours decline, those market value losses are set to get steeper. From Wednesday’s closing share price, a drop of 8% would erase another $335 billion in market value.
 Nvidia shares hit a record high on October 6, and the market value hit a peak of almost $5.8 trillion. Since then, shares have dropped more than 25% and the company has lost more than $1.5 trillion in market value.
 Apple in recent weeks overtook Nvidia as the world’s largest company by market value.

 Nvidia's Code of Conduct emphasizes ethical behavior, avoiding conflicts of interest
 By Clare Duffy 
 Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang speaks during Nvidia Live at CES 2026 ahead of the annual Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas, Nevada, on January 5, 2026. 
 Patrick T. Fallon/AFP/Getty Images 
 Nvidia’s Code of Conduct begins with a letter from CEO Jensen Huang saying that “the best and brightest can do their life’s work and build a great life and family” at the company.
 “By putting the interests of the company before our own, we can more easily accomplish Nvidia’s vision,” the code reads.
 Nvidia’s board is now weighing whether to replace Huang as CEO following reports about his extramarital relationships, including one with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.
 The document lays out how employees, business partners and managers are expected to act with integrity and avoid conflicts of interest. It notes that managers play a “special role” in “promoting equitable and ethical decisions, and fostering safe work environments.”
 “We ask ourselves what the impact would be if our conduct or action became public or came to the attention of respected colleagues,” it states.
 The document notes that violations of the code or Nvidia’s policies could lead to disciplinary action, including potential termination.
 In its most recent proxy statement filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, Nvidia wrote that its “Code of Conduct applies to all executive officers, directors, and employees, including our principal executive officer, principal financial officer, and principal accounting officer.”

 Link Copied!
 Jensen Huang spoke out against succession plans
 By Hadas Gold 
 Jensen Huang attends a press briefing in Paris on October 13. 
 Joel Saget/AFP/Getty Images/File 
 Jensen Huang famously has never believed in succession planning, telling podcaster Lex Fridman earlier this year that it’s not because he thinks he’s “immortal,” but because he believes the best way to handle such concerns is to prepare everyone at the company.
 “The most important thing you should do today if you care about the future of your company post you is to pass on knowledge, information, insight, skills, experience as often and continuously as you can, which is why I continuously reason about everything in front of my team,” Huang said, adding that he hopes he “dies on the job.”
 He is also fond of poking fun at other CEOs, telling them that when their children are running their companies, Huang would still be running Nvidia.
 In an interview filmed just a few weeks before the latest scandal broke, Huang told Bloomberg he hopes the “next leader of the company is already at the company.”
 “Just as I can be fired the next CEO has to be hired,” he added. “I like it that way. I like that we can’t be overly complacent about our position inside the company and we can’t take it for granted, and you’re always vulnerable, you’re always earning it, you’re always striving to be better.”

 Who is Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy in Jensen’s ear? 
 1:42
 It is unclear exactly where and when alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang met Nvidia chief Jensen Huang (no relation), but she had become something of a regular fixture in Jensen Huang’s business circles, appearing at his side at private and corporate events.
 The two were pictured together as early as September 2024 on WeChat, the ubiquitous Chinese social messaging app, at a luxury golf resort in California.
 Records from US Customs and Border Protection show Alice Huang has visited the US ten times since 2017. The most recent trip was in March of last year, when she was photographed visiting Nvidia headquarters in Santa Clara during the company’s annual conference.
 In May 2025, the two attended a group dinner in Taipei during a tech conference and left in the same car.
 Nvidia has previously denied there was anything “unusual or unexpected” about their relationship. But on Sunday, the company said it was opening an independent investigation into whether the CEO was “the target of a foreign intelligence effort” — the same weekend Jensen Huang admitted to his extramarital affair without naming the other party involved.
 Read our full report.

 Who is reported Chinese spy Alice Huang?
 By Stephanie Yang 
 For someone suddenly generating international headlines, Alice Huang — the woman US officials believe was working as a Chinese spy while having an affair with Nvidia chief Jensen Huang (of no relation) — remains something of a mystery.
 Her limited online footprint paints a picture of a journalist-turned tech power broker who held senior positions at financial firms in Asia.
 Here’s what we know: 
 Her identity: US Customs and Border Patrol travel records obtained by CNN that correspond with Alice Huang’s social media posts in the US identify her as a 43-year-old Chinese citizen by the name of Huang Le.
 Former reporter: According to Chinese social media and databases tracking the career of Huang Le, she worked as a journalist for Chinese state television before pivoting to a career in finance.
 Finance jobs: One Chinese private-equity fund website said Huang had four years of experience in the media and eight in the securities industry, including at HSBC and Citic Securities. CNN has reached out to HSBC and Citic Securities for comment.
 Buying AI chips: From March to November of 2023, Huang was a director at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based cloud computing and data center provider that was originally incorporated as a Chinese video game developer. In the three years since, Megaspeed has become one of the largest buyers of Nvidia chips in Asia. Corporate records also indicate Megaspeed received funding from Chinese tech giant Alibaba, and the company has come under investigation for potentially providing Chinese companies with unauthorized access to US chips. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.
 Where is she now? Her current whereabouts are unclear, and she has made no public statement or appearance since last year, when reports of the suspicions surrounding her relationship with Jensen Huang first broke. CNN has reached out to Megaspeed, Singapore’s government and Singaporean police.

 Nvidia’s over $4 trillion market value rests largely in part thanks to Jensen Huang, a key figure in the AI trade from the White House to Wall Street.
 But in the middle of a stunning scandal, Nvidia’s close link to its sole CEO highlights a major vulnerability in the AI ecosystem: the “ key man risk .”

 Both Tesla and SpaceX revolve around CEO Elon Musk , the richest person in the world.
 OpenAI is almost synonymous with Sam Altman, its mercurial CEO.
 Meta co-founder Mark Zuckerberg’s fingerprints are all over virtually every major move made by the Facebook and Instagram owner, another major AI player.

 Lack of clear succession plan raises questions about who could replace Huang
 By Clare Duffy 
 The Nvidia headquarters in Santa Clara, California, US, on Monday. 
 David Paul Morris/Bloomberg/Getty Images 
 Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been synonymous with the company he founded 33 years ago and famously doesn’t believe in succession planning.
 That could put his board in a tricky position as it meets to discuss his possible ouster.
 “Our company was built so that I know how to run it,” he told Bloomberg in 2023. “So for as long as I’m running it, that’s all that matters.”
 He expanded on that philosophy in a podcast interview with Lex Fridman earlier this year, saying that it’s not because he thinks he’s “immortal” but because he believes it’s best to prepare everyone at the company with the skills and information needed to lead. He added that he hopes he “dies on the job.”
 Nvidia’s unusual corporate structure — with Huang famously having around 60 direct reports — does not lend itself to providing a clear No. 2 that would be an obvious choice to take over for the chief executive.
 “It’s very unusual, I think, not to have a formal succession plan developed by the board in conjunction with the CEO,” David Larcker, director of the Corporate Governance Research Initiative at Stanford Graduate School of Business, told CNN.
 Still, he added, the board may have had little incentive to challenge Huang’s opposition to succession planning amid the meteoric rise of the company’s stock in recent years.
 Larcker said that “virtually every company that’s well governed is going to have an emergency candidate,” and that specific details are often considered proprietary information. Nvidia, however, has shared less information about its planning with investors than other big tech companies.
 Nvidia’s latest proxy statement mentions “succession planning” only once — compared to around a dozen times in Google and Apple’s most recent reports — in a risk disclosure noting the company is “highly dependent on the services of our longstanding executive team.”
